world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

new_statements.quote: Stress is on the penultimate syllable of the root, except for a few exceptions where stress is on the final syllable. Stress is indicated in the orthography only where it is contrastive. [p. 11] || Dalam bahasa Teiwa tekanan kata biasanya terjadi pada kata dasar (akar kata), pada suku kata satu sebelum terakhir (kedua dari belakang). Ada beberapa perkataan khusus yang mendapat tekanan pada suku terakhir. Dalam sistem tulisan tekanan biasanya tidak ditandai atau ditulis sama sekali, kecuali kalau makna kata tergantung pada tekanan [p. 7]
new_statements.translation: [Indonesian p. 7] In the Teiwa language word stress usually occurs on the base word (root), on the syllable before the last (second from the end). There are some particular words that receive stress on the last syllable. In the writing system stress is usually not marked or written at all, except when the meaning of the word depends on stress.
new_statements.citation: Klamer, Marian & Amos Sir. 2011. Kosakata bahasa Teiwa-Indonesia-Inggris / Teiwa-Indonesian-English wordlist (UBB Language & Culture Series A-6). Kupang: Unit Bahasa dan Budaya. ISBN 978-1-86892-599-5.
new_statements.locator: sec. 4.2 'Stress, affixes, pronouns', p. 11 (English); sec. 3.1.3 'Tekanan', p. 7 (Indonesian, with the minimal pairs)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root (affixes not counted); a small set of words has final stress instead, and since this creates minimal pairs the exceptions are lexically marked (written with an acute accent only when contrastive). Secondary literature by the same author characterises the system as penultimate stress mixed with weight-sensitivity (heavy final syllables attract stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: 'a few exceptions where stress is on the final syllable' (Indonesian: 'Ada beberapa perkataan khusus yang mendapat tekanan pada suku terakhir'), yielding minimal pairs bángan 'minta/ask' vs bangán 'hidup/live'; tárau 'urat, otot/sinew' vs taráu ~ trau 'bahasa/language'; día' 'sejenis rumput berduri/a thorny grass' vs -diá', nadiá' 'bahu, bahu-ku/shoulder, my shoulder'. Secondary sources (Holton & Klamer 2018: 587; Holton & Robinson 2017: 55) add that heavy syllables attract stress in Teiwa (jiˈvar 'dog'), i.e. the final-stress cases are at least partly weight-driven; the grammar (Klamer 2010, not opened) is the source for that.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/root level: stress is described on the root ('kata dasar (akar kata)'), i.e. possessor prefixes and other affixes are outside the domain. Statement is from the front matter of a wordlist, so citation forms; no phrase-level information.
new_statements.identity_note: Klamer & Sir 2011 and Klamer 2010 describe Teiwa as spoken in Madar/Lebang and neighbouring villages on Pantar (Klamer's fieldwork variety); no dialect split is named and the statement is presented for Teiwa as a whole (teiw1235). The audit422 round earlier recorded this same wordlist with sec. 4.2 at 'p. 10'; the rendered scan shows sec. 4.2 on printed p. 11 (the TOC agrees), sec. 3.1.3 on p. 7.

Also p. 156 fn.: initial-syllable loss 'may have to do with the fact that stress was apparently based on syllable weight' (historical). Comparative, second-hand for Teiwa.

sources.note: p. 587: 'Stress patterns are variable in the TAP languages. Stress may be trochaic (on the penultimate syllable, e.g. Western Pantar, Tsunaq), on the final syllable (Kaera), or be weight-sensitive (where heavy syllables are stressed) (Abui), or it may mix penultimate and weight-sensitive stress (Teiwa).' Survey chapter co-authored by the grammar's author; no page reference to Klamer 2010 given.
